newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian stocks end lower ahead of U.S. holiday.
newsitem.headline: Australian stocks end lower ahead of U.S. holiday.

text.p: The Australian stock market chalked up modest losses by the close on Friday as caution crept in ahead of the Independence Day holiday in U.S. markets.
The All Ordinaries index lost 9.5 points to 2,733.4.

The market played according to script, with the light afternoon selling widely expected by traders and gold stocks taking a hammering after news that the Reserve Bank of Australia had sold 167 tonnes of gold reserves over the past six months.
This surprise sparked sharp drops in gold stocks and pushed the sector benchmark index to its lowest close since April 1993.
"Gold stocks have been the ones in the (sellers') sights today," said a dealer at a Sydney-based investment bank.
Making up 20 percent of the gold index, Normandy Mining suffered, opening nearly nine percent lower at A$1.333 (US$1.00) before recovering ground to close 3.4 percent down at A$1.41.
Newcrest Mining slumped over six percent to A$3.20 and with Normandy topped turnover lists with over nine million shares traded in each stock.

Among others, Goldfields dived over 12 percent to A$1.66, while Acacia Resources ended 4.2 percent down at A$1.61, Emperor Mines lost over nine percent to A$1.50 and Great Central Mines lost over five percent to A$2.382.
The immediate outlook for the sector was unsettled, with traders expecting further turmoil in the precious metals sector.
"The golds and resources will become extremely volatile in the next couple of weeks, depending on what comes out," said Martin Angel of Perth-based brokerage, Eyres Reed.
The rest of the market was a mixed, patchy affair with most coming back from late morning highs as investors lightened positions in the afternoon session.
In terms of outlook, traders said with New York closed for the July 4 holiday the local market was likely to consolidate, at least early in the week, while recent rises were digested.
Falls outnumbered rises by a ratio of about nine to five, while about 24 percent of stocks traded remained steady.
